source.title: Transferring Linear Features Across Language Models With Model Stitching
source.authors: Alan Chen; Jack Merullo; Alessandro Stolfo; Ellie Pavlick

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests transfer and recovery of SAE features in language models of different sizes and families, rather than reproducing the original toy-model superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses superposition and linear features but does not train toy networks or test feature competition, polysemantic neurons, or capacity allocation. It measures SAE transfer, probe performance using transferred SAE features, feature attribution correlations, and selected feature functions. Layer choices and other setup values are not results. The language-steering results do not test the listed versions. Cited findings from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper uses SAEs and linear features as tools. It assumes they exist and are linear, then measures how well an affine stitch carries them between same-family models of different sizes. The results bear on cross-model representational universality and on the stitch method's performance. They do not show whether real models spread features across neurons or whether SAEs recover sparse features (V4). They also do not show whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units of a model (V5): every row compares a transferred SAE with its source, not the SAE with the model's own representation. No toy models, capacity tests, polysemanticity analysis or 1-D vs multi-D comparison appear.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the headline result: using a small-to-large transferred SAE as initialization cuts SAE training FLOPs by about 50%. Also, the authors say probes and steering vectors transfer without extra training only 'in specific cases'. Instruction-following steering transfer was weak.
record.recipe_differences: Uses affine model stitches and cross-model SAE transfer, not the original toy-network setup or its feature-geometry interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Transferability varies by feature class and probing dataset; code and language probing is harder without probe retraining. The authors also report weaker instruction-following steering than language steering, but that steering result is not a row for these claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Affine stitches between same-family models of different sizes transfer SAEs, probes and steering vectors with partial fidelity. Transferred SAE FUV is 0.39–0.52 vs 0.11–0.21 for the source SAEs (r1–r6). Structural features transfer more consistently than semantic ones (r13–r16), and some functional features keep their roles (r17–r20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak representational universality: models of different size in one family share linear feature spaces that an affine map can largely align.

fits_no_version.finding: Initializing an SAE on the larger model from a stitch-transferred SAE reaches high explained-variance thresholds with about 30–50% fewer FLOPs. Decoder vectors also rotate less during training than from random initialization (Fig. 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak universality can be exploited to cut SAE training cost.

record.problems: The authors state that the semantic/structural classification can be noisy because augmentations are generated by another language model, and that feature transferability is assessed correlationally. Probing and steering evaluations are limited to particular tasks and settings. Transferred SAE evaluations are worse than fully trained destination-model SAEs. Several relevant feature-transfer results are presented only as plots without exact values.
record.rows_left_out: Steering-vector response-language and instruction-following outcomes were omitted because they measure induced steering rather than the versions' named feature-storage or SAE-unit claims. Dense-probe results were omitted because they do not use SAE features. No other claim-relevant reported results were left out.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition or feature geometry.
No capacity competition or dedicated-vs-shared dimension analysis.
No analysis of the causes of polysemantic neurons.
Uses pretrained and trained SAEs without testing whether features are distributed across neurons or whether SAEs recover true sparse features.
Does not test completeness, stability across seeds or widths, or canonicality of SAE features within a model. Cross-model transfer bears on universality, not on this version.
Assumes linear 1-D features; no comparison with multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T3 classification overreads the study. The paper relies on the linear-representation and SAE framing and evaluates its stitching method, so it is uses_without_test/T4. All rows are relinked to 'none'. They remain useful under a universality claim rather than under the superposition versions.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
Does not test whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests SAE-feature probing and transfer, but not whether real-model features are distributed across many neurons.
Tests transferability of selected SAE features and feature-level measures across model pairs; does not establish completeness, uniqueness, or canonicality of SAE features.
Uses vector-valued SAE features but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: pythia-160m-deduped
rows.operation_detail: Used selected features from a transferred SAE as sparse probes without retraining the probe.
rows.baseline: Random features; exact values not stated
rows.value: The paper reports successful probing without probe retraining and performance significantly better than random in most datasets; exact values figure only.
rows.note: The paper says code and language datasets are exceptions to the generally successful no-retraining results.
rows.check: Probe transfer accuracy vs random features is a downstream application of the stitch. It does not test whether SAEs recover sparse features.

rows.subject: pythia-160m-deduped
rows.operation_detail: Retrained probes using the same features from the transferred SAE.
rows.baseline: Ground-truth SAE features on Pythia-160m; exact values not stated
rows.value: The paper reports that retraining almost recovers ground-truth performance; exact values figure only.
rows.note: Recovery is described as nearly, not fully, matching ground-truth performance.
rows.check: Retrained-probe accuracy vs a ground-truth SAE is a stitch-application result. It is not about superposition or canonicality.

rows.subject: gpt2-medium
rows.operation_detail: Used features from transferred GPT2 SAE probes, without and with probe retraining.
rows.baseline: Random features and ground-truth GPT2-medium SAE; exact values not stated
rows.value: The paper reports better-than-random probing with transferred features; code and language domains are hard without retraining and improve with retraining; exact values figure only.
rows.note: The appendix describes results as similar to Pythia and identifies code and language as transfer difficulties.
rows.check: GPT2 probe transfer, figure only. It is a stitch-application result.

rows.subject: pythia-160m-deduped
rows.operation_detail: Compared attribution correlations for features under the stitch with a random-SAE comparison.
rows.baseline: Random SAE comparison; exact values figure only
rows.value: Most features do better than a random stitch, but some are flipped or transfer poorly; exact values figure only.
rows.note: The paper describes the comparison qualitatively and shows distributions rather than tabulated values.
rows.check: Attribution-correlation distribution vs a random SAE measures cross-model feature transfer, which is universality, not a version.

rows.subject: gpt2-medium
rows.operation_detail: Measured properties of two entropy SAE features before and after transfer.

rows.subject: gpt2-medium
rows.operation_detail: Measured properties of two entropy SAE features before and after transfer.
rows.measure: Fraction of norm in effective null space
rows.baseline: Original features in gpt2-small; exact values figure only
rows.value: After transfer, the features still compose highly with the effective null space; exact values figure only.
rows.note: The effective null space is defined as the bottom 2% of singular values.
rows.check: Preservation of null-space composition under transfer is a functional-universality case study.

rows.subject: gpt2-medium
rows.operation_detail: Path-zero-ablated the transferred feature's contribution to a downstream attention head input and measured attention to BOS.
rows.measure: Change in attention to the BOS token after zero-ablation
rows.baseline: Feature contribution present; exact values figure only
rows.value: Zero-ablating the transferred feature decreases attention to BOS for the plotted tokens; exact values figure only.
rows.note: The authors identify the transferred feature as retaining its attention-deactivation role.
rows.check: Attention-deactivation role kept after transfer is a functional-universality case study. The text also notes the same feature acts as an activator for another head (Fig. 16).

rows.subject: gpt2-medium
rows.operation_detail: Measured the attention deactivation feature's component in the effective null space before and after transfer.
rows.measure: Fraction of norm in effective null space
rows.baseline: 0.27 (original)
rows.value: 0.77 (stitch)
rows.note: The paper states that this property is preserved and gives the original and transferred values.
rows.check: Null-space fraction 0.27 vs 0.77 is a property of a transferred feature, not a version's effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Transferred SAE-feature probes on the tested Pythia and GPT2 datasets
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports probing better than random with transferred SAE features, and reports that retraining the probes nearly recovers ground-truth performance (r7–r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Cross-model SAE transfer quality and feature-class results
reader_labels.reason: Transferred SAEs have worse FUV and Delta Loss than their source SAEs, and transfer differs across features and datasets, including difficult code/language probes (r1–r6, r13–r16).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tested cross-model feature transfer and selected functional features
reader_labels.reason: Some features and feature classes transfer well or retain selected functions, but others are flipped, transfer poorly, or are left behind; the paper does not establish SAE features as complete or canonical units (r10–r20).
